children: The Australian dollar hit an 11-month low on Friday, pressured by a relentless slide in global stocks, falling commodity prices and the prospects of steady domestic interest rates, while the kiwi plumbed a six-year trough.
slipped 0.2% to $0.6647, the lowest since December 2025 and down for a ninth straight session. It slid 0.8% overnight, breaking key support around $0.6662 and bears are now targeting $0.6593.
For the week, it is down 1.8%, the third straight week of declines.

Markets are betting that interest rates in Australia have peaked at 4.85% after a shockingly weak jobs report raised fears that the economy might be entering a sharp downturn. Sticky inflation meant no quick rate relief, but the market has fully priced in a first rate cut for August next year. (0#AUDIRPR)
The spread between Australia's 10-year government bond yield and Treasuries has now turned negative by 6 basis points, down from a positive 80 bps in March, eroding the Aussie's yield support.

"The market is pricing another three 25bp increases in the US by mid‑2027. By contrast, the market is pricing one and a half 25bp decreases in Australia by the end of 2027," said Joseph Capurso, head of international economics at the Commonwealth Bank of Australia.
"The convergence in Australian and US interest rates will continue to be a weight on AUD/USD for months ahead."

Renee Fry-McKibbin, an external board member at the Reserve Bank of Australia, said on Friday she saw pockets of strong demand in the Australian economy, but weakness elsewhere as policymaking became more difficult.
In New Zealand, the kiwi dollar
was last steady at $0.5486, having hit a six-year low of $0.5475 earlier in the session. It is set for a 0.7% weekly drop, its fourth week of declines, with support fragile at $0.5469.

Swaps now imply a 78% probability that the Reserve Bank of New Zealand will raise interest rates by a quarter percentage point to 3%, with 80 basis points of tightening priced in by the end of next year. (0#NZDIRPR)
The Aussie lost 1.1% this week to NZ$1.2119
, its lowest since September, as the policy outlooks for the two central banks diverged.
